cases.title: Fire Response Using RACE Principles
cases.stem: On a rehabilitation unit, a staff member smells smoke near a patient room and sees a small electrical fire beginning at a portable warmer that had been brought in without proper approval. Several patients on the unit have mobility limitations, and one is receiving oxygen therapy nearby. The nurse must act rapidly to protect patients and staff while following institutional fire safety principles. Panic and delay could increase injury risk, especially for vulnerable patients who cannot evacuate independently.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which features make this an immediate fire safety emergency? Select all that apply.

options.text: Visible smoke and ignition source
Mobility-limited patients on the unit
Oxygen therapy nearby
Unapproved electrical equipment
Need for rapid structured response

questions.rationale: All these factors increase risk. Oxygen therapy and reduced patient mobility can make even a small fire much more dangerous.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The staff should wait to see if the smoke clears
The unit requires immediate structured fire response according to safety protocol
Only maintenance staff should respond
Fire safety is less urgent than finishing medication rounds

questions.rationale: Fire response requires immediate action according to protocol. Delay may place multiple patients at risk.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for smoke inhalation, burn injury, and rapid spread of harm to vulnerable patients
Disturbed sleep pattern
Missed lunch break
Mild inconvenience

questions.rationale: The immediate concern is preventing injury and protecting vulnerable patients from smoke and fire.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Begin the RACE response by protecting patients in immediate danger, activating the alarm, and following the next protocol steps
Finish charting before responding
Leave patients in place until someone else arrives
Ignore the small fire if it seems contained

questions.rationale: Fire response must be prompt and structured. RACE provides a clear priority sequence to protect patients and staff.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Move or protect those at greatest immediate risk first
Be aware of oxygen-related hazards near the fire area
Follow facility policy regarding containment and extinguisher use if appropriate and safe
Keep exits and evacuation routes clear
Assume mobility-limited patients can self-evacuate without assistance

questions.rationale: These are all correct. Nurses must consider who is least able to self-protect in an emergency.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective fire response?

options.text: Patients at immediate risk are protected, the alarm is activated, spread is limited, and evacuation or containment proceeds safely
Smoke spreads because staff hesitate and do nothing
Oxygen-dependent patients remain beside the fire source
Policy is ignored because the fire looks small

questions.rationale: Effective fire response is organised, fast, and focused on immediate patient protection.

cases.title: Wrong-Patient Medication Near Miss
cases.stem: On a busy morning, two patients with similar surnames are assigned to adjacent beds. One is due for insulin and the other is due for an antihypertensive medication. A nurse approaches the bedside with medications prepared and is about to administer them after asking only, “Are you Mr. Taylor?” The patient nods, distracted by television. At the last moment, another nurse notices the chart in hand belongs to the other patient. The event is a near miss that highlights the critical role of two identifiers and medication verification.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which factors created wrong-patient medication risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Similar surnames in nearby beds
Only one verbal identifier used
Distracted patient response
Medications prepared before full bedside verification
Near miss detected just before administration

questions.rationale: All of these contributed to risk. Similar names and incomplete identifier use are classic medication safety traps.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient’s nod was enough confirmation
A serious wrong-patient medication near miss occurred and safe identifier practice failed
Near misses do not matter because no medication was given
Similar names are unavoidable and cannot be managed

questions.rationale: Near misses matter because they reveal unsafe systems or practice gaps before harm occurs. Two identifiers are essential.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for wrong-patient medication administration due to identification failure
Disturbed sleep pattern
Delayed breakfast service
Social isolation

questions.rationale: Wrong-patient medication administration can cause significant harm and must be prevented through strict identification practices.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the process, verify identity using two approved identifiers, and restart medication administration safely
Give the medications because the patient already nodded
Ask the roommate to confirm identity
Chart the medications as administered to save time

questions.rationale: The near miss must be corrected immediately by proper patient verification. Roommates or nods are not acceptable identifiers.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Report the near miss according to policy
Reinforce unit practices for patients with similar names
Review the medication administration process for vulnerabilities
Document accurately and continue to use two identifiers every time
Assume that because no drug was given, no learning is needed

questions.rationale: Near misses are valuable safety data. They should be reported and used to improve process reliability.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The near miss is corrected before administration, reported appropriately, and safer identification practice is reinforced on the unit
Staff dismiss the event because no harm occurred
Similar-name safeguards are not reviewed
Single-identifier practice continues

questions.rationale: Safety culture depends on learning from near misses as well as actual errors.

cases.title: Mandatory Reporting and Unsafe Practice by an Impaired Coworker
cases.stem: During an evening shift, a nurse notices that a coworker appears unusually drowsy, is slurring words slightly, and nearly gives medication to the wrong patient before being interrupted. Later, the same coworker struggles to calculate a simple dosage and asks to borrow someone else’s login to fix charting quickly. The observing nurse feels uneasy because the colleague is well liked and has recently gone through personal difficulties. However, patient safety may be at serious risk if impairment is affecting practice. The nurse must balance professionalism, reporting duty, and prevention of harm.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings indicate a potential impaired-practice safety issue? Select all that apply.

options.text: Slurred speech and drowsiness
Near wrong-patient medication administration
Difficulty with simple dosage calculation
Request to use someone else’s login
Repeated unsafe behaviour during the shift

questions.rationale: All these findings suggest serious impairment or unsafe practice. The issue must be addressed because patient safety is at risk.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Personal problems mean the coworker should be left alone
The colleague may be impaired or unsafe to practice, requiring immediate reporting through proper channels
Friendship should outweigh safety concerns
Only the final error matters, not the pattern of near misses

questions.rationale: The nurse’s duty is to protect patients. Reporting unsafe practice is an ethical and legal safety responsibility.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for patient harm due to unsafe clinical performance by an impaired coworker
Social discomfort between coworkers
Disturbed work friendships
Shift scheduling problems

questions.rationale: Patient safety is the priority. Personal discomfort must not override professional duty.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the immediate patient safety risk by reporting the concern to the appropriate supervisor promptly and factually
Ignore the behaviour for one more shift
Cover up the errors to protect the coworker
Publicly shame the coworker in front of patients

questions.rationale: Unsafe practice requires prompt factual reporting through the correct chain of command. Public humiliation is not the appropriate response.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Document objective observations according to policy if required
Focus on patient safety rather than personal judgment about the coworker
Prevent unauthorized use of another staff member’s login
Cooperate with follow-up processes to protect patients
Assume near misses do not require action

questions.rationale: All of these support a professional safety response. Objective reporting is key; assumptions or gossip are not.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The unsafe practice concern is reported promptly, immediate patient risk is reduced, and the issue is handled through proper safety channels
The coworker continues making errors because no one wanted conflict
Staff share rumours instead of reporting appropriately
Login misuse continues unchecked

questions.rationale: Effective management protects patients and handles the issue through formal safety processes.

cases.title: Disaster Triage in a Multi-Casualty Event
cases.stem: Following a bus collision, multiple injured patients arrive rapidly at a small emergency department. Resources are limited, and the triage nurse must make fast decisions. One adult is walking and crying with a bleeding arm wound, another is not breathing until repositioned, and a third is unconscious with severe head trauma and weak pulses. Several others have fractures and moderate pain. The nurse must apply mass-casualty triage principles rather than usual one-patient-at-a-time priorities. Safety, resource allocation, and rapid categorization are essential.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which features are central in mass-casualty triage? Select all that apply.

options.text: Limited resources compared with patient volume
Need to sort by survivability and urgency
Different prioritisation than standard bedside care
Walking wounded may be categorized differently
Airway opening response may rapidly change triage priority

questions.rationale: All these are true. Disaster triage requires rapid sorting based on urgency and likelihood of benefit from immediate intervention, not routine one-on-one care patterns.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Standard detailed full assessments should be completed on each patient before triage
Rapid triage frameworks such as START/SALT are needed to prioritise care safely in this setting
The loudest patient is always the highest priority
Only physicians can triage in disaster situations

questions.rationale: Mass-casualty situations require rapid, structured triage. The loudest or most visible patient is not always the sickest.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Need to rapidly allocate limited resources to maximize survival and prevent avoidable deaths
Ensuring everyone is seen in arrival order
Avoiding any emotional discomfort for staff
Providing full discharge teaching immediately

questions.rationale: The purpose of disaster triage is to maximize safe and effective use of limited resources.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Begin rapid triage using approved disaster principles, identifying who can walk, who needs immediate airway/life-saving attention, and who can wait briefly
Perform a full medication reconciliation on the first patient
Treat the bleeding arm wound first because it is obvious
Delay triage until every chart is prepared

questions.rationale: Rapid categorisation comes first. Disaster response requires concise, lifesaving prioritisation rather than full routine assessment.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassess triage categories as patient condition changes
Communicate clearly with the team using the chosen triage framework
Keep safety and scene organization in mind
Direct ambulatory patients to a designated safer area if appropriate
Assume triage labels never need updating

questions.rationale: Disaster triage is dynamic. Patients may worsen or improve, so reassessment is important.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective triage management?

options.text: Patients are sorted rapidly and logically, the most salvageable critical cases receive immediate attention, and team coordination remains organized
All patients are treated strictly by arrival order
No one is reassessed after initial labeling
Staff spend too long on one moderate injury while critical cases wait

questions.rationale: Effective disaster triage balances speed, organization, and lifesaving prioritisation.

cases.title: Early Sepsis Recognition and Escalation
cases.stem: Mr. Aaron Matthews, a 61-year-old patient with pneumonia, initially appears stable on the ward. Over several hours, the nurse notices subtle changes: increasing confusion, respiratory rate 28, temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 124, blood pressure falling from baseline, and urine output lower than expected. Family members say, “He seems more confused than this morning.” The nurse realises that infection may be progressing toward sepsis. Early recognition and escalation are vital because delaying action can rapidly increase morbidity and mortality.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings suggest possible sepsis progression? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fever
Tachycardia and tachypnoea
New confusion
Decreasing blood pressure from baseline
Reduced urine output

questions.rationale: All of these are important sepsis warning signs. New confusion and low urine output often indicate worsening perfusion and organ dysfunction.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient is just tired from pneumonia
The patient may be progressing to sepsis and requires urgent reassessment and escalation
Confusion is unrelated to infection
Vital sign changes should be ignored until the next round

questions.rationale: The pattern is concerning for sepsis, not routine fatigue. NCLEX safety questions heavily test early recognition of deterioration.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for impaired tissue perfusion and organ dysfunction related to sepsis
Disturbed sleep pattern
Nutrition knowledge deficit
Social isolation

questions.rationale: Sepsis threatens multiple organ systems. Early intervention is essential to prevent shock and failure.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Escalate urgently, reassess the patient comprehensively, and prepare for sepsis-related interventions according to protocol
Wait to see if the confusion resolves spontaneously
Focus only on reducing fever with comfort measures
Delay reporting until the next doctor round

questions.rationale: The nurse should respond to the trend immediately. Sepsis care is time-sensitive and requires urgent action.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor blood pressure, urine output, and mental status closely
Prepare for cultures, fluids, and timely antimicrobial-related steps as ordered or protocol-based
Communicate the trend clearly using structured handover
Continue watching for worsening respiratory distress
Assume confusion is unimportant if the fever is treated

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. Confusion is an important sign of deterioration and should never be dismissed.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Sepsis concern is escalated early, treatment begins promptly, and perfusion/mental status trends are followed closely
Hypotension worsens because signs were not reported
Monitoring is reduced after one intervention
Urine output continues falling with no reassessment

questions.rationale: Effective sepsis management depends on early recognition, rapid escalation, and continuous reassessment.
